cases.cc: My belly has hurt since last night and now it's worse on the right.
hx: Around the belly button, then it moved to the lower right over a few hours.
None at all since yesterday. He felt sick and threw up once, after the pain started.
Yes, the car ride in hurt every bump.
Any diarrhea or blood in stool?
Pain when peeing or blood in urine?
ex: Press on the right lower quadrant
Sharp tenderness at McBurney's point (one third from the hip bone to the navel).
Pain is felt in the RIGHT lower quadrant (Rovsing sign).
Hurts (psoas sign): an inflamed appendix lies on the psoas muscle.
Listen to the heart and lungs
Tap the back over the kidneys
tx: Ultrasound of the right lower quadrant
Non-compressible tubular structure, 9 mm wide, with fluid around it.
Dilated appendix with fat stranding. (Fine, but ultrasound or CT, not both, in a young patient.)
Normal. Nothing in the story pointed to the head.
cases.patho: The appendix lumen gets blocked (often by a hardened stool pellet called a fecalith, or swollen lymph tissue). Mucus builds up, pressure rises, blood flow drops and bacteria invade the wall. Early pain is vague and central because visceral pain fibres enter the cord at T10 (the navel dermatome). Once the inflamed appendix touches the parietal peritoneum, somatic nerves give sharp, localised right lower quadrant pain. Untreated, the wall dies and can perforate (usually after 48–72 h).
tr: Surgery: laparoscopic appendectomy is standard.
IV fluids, nothing by mouth, pain relief (opioid analgesics are fine and don't hide the diagnosis).
Antibiotics: broad-spectrum IV cover for gut bacteria (e.g. a cephalosporin plus metronidazole class) before surgery; some uncomplicated cases are treated with antibiotics alone.
cases.pearl: Migration of pain (navel → right lower quadrant) plus anorexia is the most useful history combo. Alvarado score adds them up.

cases.cc: She's been throwing up and breathing really fast, and she's so tired.
cases.vit: T 37.2 °C · HR 122 · BP 98/60 · RR 32, deep · SpO₂ 99%
hx: Has she been drinking or peeing a lot?
Yes, constantly thirsty and up at night to pee for 3 weeks.
Lost about 4 kg this month without trying.
Yes, diffuse cramping since this morning.
ex: Fruity, like nail-polish remover (acetone from ketones).
Deep, sighing, rapid breaths: Kussmaul respiration (blowing off CO₂ to fight acidosis).
Dry lips, capillary refill 3 s: dehydrated.
Drowsy but answers questions. No focal signs.
tx: pH 7.08, bicarbonate 7 mmol/L: severe metabolic acidosis.
Sodium 131, potassium 5.6, anion gap 28, creatinine slightly high.
Normal. Not needed while she's talking normally.
Normal. Belly pain in DKA usually settles with treatment.
cases.patho: With almost no insulin, cells can't take up glucose, so the body acts as if it is starving. Glucagon and stress hormones push the liver to make more glucose and break fat into ketone bodies (acetoacetate, β-hydroxybutyrate), which are acids. Glucose spills into urine and drags water with it (osmotic diuresis), causing thirst, peeing and dehydration. The acid load drops pH and bicarbonate (high anion gap), and the lungs compensate with deep Kussmaul breathing. Total body potassium is low even if the blood level looks high, because acidosis and no insulin shift potassium out of cells.
tr: IV fluids first (isotonic crystalloid) to restore volume.
Insulin as a continuous IV infusion to stop ketone production; add dextrose to the drip once glucose falls.
Potassium replacement guided by levels (insulin drives potassium back into cells).
Find the trigger (infection, missed insulin) and teach long-term insulin therapy.
cases.pearl: In kids, cerebral edema is the feared complication: rehydrate steadily, not too fast, and watch for headache or confusion.

cases.cc: I suddenly couldn't catch my breath and my chest hurts when I breathe in.
cases.vit: T 37.4 °C · HR 118 · BP 116/74 · RR 26 · SpO₂ 90% on room air
hx: Flew back from Australia (14 h) four days ago.
Her left calf has been sore and puffy since the flight.
A little blood-streaked sputum this morning.
Takes an estrogen-containing pill; doesn't smoke.
ex: Left calf 3 cm wider than the right, tender along the deep veins.
Clear, maybe a quiet area at the right base.
Not tender (so it's not just a strained muscle).
tx: Sinus tachycardia; S wave in I, Q wave and inverted T in III (S1Q3T3), which is uncommon but classic.
Mostly normal. Normal X-ray + low oxygen is a big clue.
Filling defects in the right and left lower lobe pulmonary arteries.
High. (Only useful to RULE OUT when the probability is low; here go straight to CT.)
Clot in the left popliteal vein.
cases.patho: A deep vein thrombosis forms in the leg (Virchow's triad: stasis from the long flight, hypercoagulability from estrogen, endothelial injury). A piece breaks off, travels through the right heart and lodges in the pulmonary arteries. Lung tissue that is ventilated but not perfused creates dead space, and blood shunted elsewhere causes hypoxemia. Pressure in the pulmonary artery rises, straining the right ventricle (troponin, loud P2, S1Q3T3). Small peripheral clots infarct the lung surface, causing pleuritic pain and blood in sputum.
tr: Anticoagulation: heparins or direct oral anticoagulants (factor Xa inhibitors) stop the clot from growing while the body breaks it down.
Massive PE with shock: thrombolytics (clot-busting enzymes) or catheter/surgical embolectomy.
Oxygen; stop the estrogen pill.
cases.pearl: Wells score first. Low probability → D-dimer to rule out. High probability → CT pulmonary angiogram.

cases.cc: The worst headache, a fever, and the light hurts my eyes.
hx: Over about 8 hours, getting steadily worse (not a thunderclap).
Hurts to bend his head forward.
In a crowded dorm. A dorm-mate was hospitalised last week.
His roommate says he's been mixing up words.
ex: Pain and resistance; his knees lift (Brudzinski sign).
Small purple spots on the legs that don't fade when pressed: petechiae.
Shine a light in the eyes
Pupils equal and reactive. Bright light hurts.
Check the back of the eye
tx: Drawn before antibiotics (results take a day: gram-negative diplococci grow).
Cloudy, raised pressure, white cells 2,400 (mostly neutrophils), protein high 2.1 g/L, glucose 1.1 mmol/L (low). Gram stain: gram-negative diplococci.
Normal. Only needed before LP if there's papilloedema, focal deficit, seizure or reduced consciousness.
cases.patho: Neisseria meningitidis colonises the throat, invades the blood (meningococcemia) and crosses into the subarachnoid space. Bacterial products trigger a huge immune response: neutrophils pour into the CSF, protein leaks across the inflamed barrier, and bacteria plus white cells consume glucose. Inflamed meninges cause neck stiffness and photophobia. Endotoxin in the blood damages vessels (petechiae, low platelets, DIC) and can cause shock and adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse–Friderichsen).
tr: Antibiotics immediately, ideally within an hour (don't wait for the CT or LP): a third-generation cephalosporin, plus vancomycin class cover until sensitivities are back.
Corticosteroids (dexamethasone class) given with or before the first antibiotic reduce hearing loss and neuro damage.
Fluids and support for shock; prophylactic antibiotics for close contacts.
cases.pearl: Fever + headache + stiff neck + altered mental status: most patients have at least 2 of 4. Petechial rash = meningococcus until proven otherwise.

cases.cc: He suddenly couldn't talk properly and his right arm went weak at breakfast.
cases.vit: T 36.8 °C · HR 92, irregular · BP 178/96 · RR 16 · SpO₂ 97%
hx: Exactly when was he last normal?
7:40 AM, talking at the table. Now it's 8:35 AM.
Told he has an irregular heartbeat last year, stopped his blood thinner.
A glass of wine on weekends.
ex: Ask him to speak and repeat
Halting, effortful speech; understands commands: expressive (Broca) aphasia.
Check face, arm and leg strength
Right lower face droops (forehead spared); right arm 2/5, right leg 4/5.
6.8 mmol/L (normal, so low sugar isn't faking a stroke).
tx: No bleed. Subtle loss of grey-white distinction in the left frontal lobe.
Occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery (M1 segment).
Not indicated and would delay treatment.
Useful later for prevention, not now.
cases.patho: Atrial fibrillation lets blood pool in the left atrial appendage, where a clot forms. It embolises to the left middle cerebral artery, the vessel supplying the lateral frontal and parietal cortex (face and arm motor strip, Broca's area in the dominant hemisphere). Brain cells in the core die within minutes; the surrounding penumbra is starving but salvageable if flow returns quickly. 'Time is brain': roughly 1.9 million neurons are lost every minute of a large vessel occlusion. Upper motor neuron facial weakness spares the forehead because the upper face has input from both hemispheres.
tr: Thrombolysis with a tissue plasminogen activator (alteplase/tenecteplase class) within 4.5 h of last known well if there's no bleed or contraindication.
Mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion (like M1), up to 24 h in selected patients.
Later: anticoagulation for AF (factor Xa inhibitors), statins, BP control; stroke rehab.
cases.pearl: Last known well, not when symptoms were found, starts the clock. CT first to exclude bleeding.

cases.cc: It was like being hit in the back of the head with a bat, the worst headache of my life.
hx: How quickly did it reach full strength?
Instantly, within seconds, while lifting a box.
Did she pass out or vomit?
A milder sudden headache two weeks ago that went away (a sentinel bleed).
Her mother had a 'brain aneurysm' and polycystic kidneys run in the family.
ex: Stiff neck (blood irritates the meninges, usually after a few hours).
Left pupil slightly larger, left eyelid droops: compression of CN III by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.
Look at the back of the eye
tx: Blood in the basal cisterns and Sylvian fissures (star-shaped hyperdensity).
7 mm aneurysm at the left posterior communicating artery.
Not needed now: CT already shows blood. (If CT were normal after 6 h, LP looks for xanthochromia.)
Deep inverted T waves (brain-heart effect); troponin normal.
cases.patho: A saccular (berry) aneurysm at a branch point of the circle of Willis ruptures, spraying arterial blood into the subarachnoid space. Intracranial pressure spikes instantly (thunderclap pain, fainting). Blood irritates the meninges and can block CSF drainage (hydrocephalus). Days 3–14 bring vasospasm: arteries bathed in blood breakdown products constrict and can cause delayed ischemic stroke. Re-bleeding is the biggest early killer, so the aneurysm must be secured quickly.
tr: Secure the aneurysm early: endovascular coiling or surgical clipping (a neurosurgery classic).
Calcium channel blocker of the dihydropyridine class (nimodipine) to improve outcome from vasospasm.
Control blood pressure, external ventricular drain for hydrocephalus, ICU monitoring.
cases.pearl: Thunderclap = peak within 1 minute. CT within 6 h of onset is nearly 100% sensitive.

cases.cc: My legs feel weak and tingly, and it's climbing up. Today I can barely climb stairs.
hx: Any illness in the past weeks?
Bad diarrhea 2 weeks ago after a barbecue (Campylobacter is a common trigger).
Feet, then legs, now his hands feel clumsy: ascending.
None (early bladder failure would suggest the spinal cord instead).
A bit short of breath lying flat.
ex: Absent at ankles and knees, reduced in the arms (areflexia).
Mild glove-and-stocking tingling; no sensory level on the trunk.
Mild weakness of both sides of the face.
Look for a tick on the scalp
tx: Protein high 1.6 g/L, white cells 2: 'albuminocytologic dissociation'.
Slowed conduction and conduction block: demyelinating neuropathy.
Normal cord (rules out compression); nerve roots enhance.
Normal potassium (rules out a potassium cause of weakness).
Normal. Not helpful in a peripheral nerve disease.
Not useful; that's for myasthenia, and largely retired.
cases.patho: After an infection, antibodies made against the microbe cross-react with molecules on peripheral nerve myelin or axons (molecular mimicry; Campylobacter LPS mimics gangliosides). Macrophages strip myelin from nerve roots and nerves, slowing or blocking conduction. Long nerves fail first, so weakness climbs from the feet. Reflex arcs break, so reflexes vanish. Autonomic fibres are hit too, causing swinging BP and heart rate. The phrenic nerves can fail, so breathing must be watched closely.
tr: Immunotherapy: IV immunoglobulin (IVIG) or plasma exchange (plasmapheresis). Steroids do NOT help in GBS.
Monitor forced vital capacity; intubate if it falls below ~20 mL/kg.
Clot prevention (low-molecular-weight heparins), pain control, physio.
cases.pearl: Rule of 20-30-40: intubate if FVC <20 mL/kg, max inspiratory pressure weaker than -30, or expiratory pressure <40.

cases.cc: My right eye has been blurry and it hurts to move it for 3 days.
hx: Yes, an ache behind the eye when she looks around.
Red looks washed out with the right eye.
Any earlier episodes of numbness or weakness?
A year ago her left leg was numb for 2 weeks and got better on its own.
Electric shock down the spine when bending the neck?
Vision dims in hot showers (Uhthoff phenomenon).
ex: Right pupil dilates when the light swings to it: relative afferent pupillary defect.
Normal-looking disc (the inflammation is behind the eye: retrobulbar neuritis).
Brisk in the left leg, left Babinski upgoing.
tx: MRI brain and spine with gadolinium
Multiple white-matter lesions around the ventricles (perpendicular 'Dawson fingers'), one enhancing (new) and others not (old): dissemination in time and space.
Oligoclonal bands present in CSF but not in serum.
Usually normal in MS; MRI is the test.
Normal; only needed if sarcoidosis is suspected.
cases.patho: Autoreactive T cells cross the blood-brain barrier and, with B cells and macrophages, attack CNS myelin made by oligodendrocytes. Demyelinated axons conduct slowly or fail (and fail more when warm: Uhthoff). Plaques form in white matter: around ventricles, optic nerves, brainstem and spinal cord. Early, remyelination lets function recover (relapsing-remitting); over time axons are lost and disability builds. The optic nerve is CNS tissue, so optic neuritis is a common first sign.
tr: Acute relapse: high-dose corticosteroids (methylprednisolone class) speed recovery.
Disease-modifying therapies: interferon-beta, anti-CD20 monoclonal antibodies, S1P receptor modulators, and others reduce relapses.
Symptom care: physio, bladder management, treat spasticity with muscle relaxants (GABA-B agonists).
cases.pearl: MS = lesions disseminated in time AND space (McDonald criteria). Oligoclonal bands can substitute for time.

cases.cc: My eyelids droop and I see double, mostly in the evening.
hx: Worse by evening and after reading; better after sleep (fatigability).
ex: Ask her to look up for 60 seconds
Ice pack on the eyelid for 2 minutes
Normal, reactive (pupils are spared in MG, unlike CN III palsy).
tx: Decrement of over 10% in muscle response.
Enlarged thymus (thymic hyperplasia or thymoma: look for it in every patient).
Normal; done only if the picture is atypical.
cases.patho: Antibodies against the postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptor block it, cross-link it (so it's internalised) and activate complement, which damages the endplate folds. Each nerve impulse releases a normal amount of ACh, but fewer receptors means a smaller endplate potential. With repeated firing, ACh release naturally declines, so more fibres fail to reach threshold: fatigable weakness. Eye muscles fail first because they have a small safety margin. The thymus is involved in making these autoantibodies.
tr: Symptomatic: acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (pyridostigmine) keep ACh in the cleft longer.
Immunotherapy: corticosteroids, steroid-sparing immunosuppressants, and complement or FcRn inhibitors.
Thymectomy (surgery) helps many patients; myasthenic crisis gets IVIG or plasma exchange and ventilator support.
cases.pearl: Avoid drugs that worsen MG: aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, magnesium, some beta-blockers.

cases.cc: He hit his head, got up and was fine. Now he's confused and sleepy.
cases.vit: T 36.9 °C · HR 54 · BP 168/92 · RR 10, irregular · SpO₂ 95%
hx: Fell, hit the side of his head (temple) on a curb, no helmet. Knocked out for ~1 minute.
What happened after he woke up?
Totally normal for about 2 hours, joking around. Then he got a headache and became drowsy.
ex: Right pupil dilated and sluggish (uncal herniation compressing CN III).
Kept still in a collar until cleared.
Slow and strong (part of Cushing's triad).
tx: Biconvex (lens-shaped) bright collection over the right temporal lobe that doesn't cross suture lines, midline shift 8 mm; skull fracture over the temporal bone.
NEVER with raised pressure and a mass: can cause herniation.
cases.patho: A fracture of the thin temporal bone (pterion) tears the middle meningeal artery. Arterial blood strips the dura away from the skull, but the dura is stuck at the sutures, so the clot bulges inward as a lens shape. After the initial knock-out, there's a 'lucid interval' while the clot grows. Then pressure rises fast: the temporal lobe uncus herniates over the tentorium, compressing CN III (blown pupil, same side) and the cerebral peduncle (weakness on the opposite side). Cushing's triad (high BP, slow heart, irregular breathing) means herniation is happening.
tr: Emergency craniotomy and evacuation of the clot by a neurosurgeon (a classic, often life-saving operation), coagulating the bleeding artery.
While waiting: head up 30°, airway protection, osmotic therapy (mannitol or hypertonic saline) to lower ICP.
Good outcomes if operated on before brainstem damage.
cases.pearl: Epidural = lens-shaped, doesn't cross sutures, arterial. Subdural = crescent, crosses sutures, venous (bridging veins).

cases.cc: My head is pounding on one side and I'm seeing zig-zag lights.
hx: Zig-zag shimmering lights spread across her vision for 20 minutes, then the headache built over an hour.
Is it the worst ever, did it hit instantly?
No; she's had 'smaller ones like this' about once a month.
Wants a dark quiet room, feels sick.
ex: Check the back of the eye
tx: A typical migraine with a normal exam and no red flags doesn't need imaging.
Normal. Adds radiation without changing anything here: an unnecessary test.
Normal. Only if red flags or an atypical pattern.
Normal (giant cell arteritis is a concern only over age 50).
Not needed: aura is not a seizure here.
cases.patho: The aura is cortical spreading depression: a slow wave (about 3 mm/min) of neuronal depolarisation followed by silence, crossing the visual cortex, which is why the zig-zags drift and spread. The headache comes from activation of the trigeminovascular system: trigeminal nerve fibres around meningeal vessels release CGRP and other peptides, causing neurogenic inflammation and sensitisation. Brainstem and thalamic sensitisation explains why light, sound and movement hurt.
tr: Acute: NSAIDs or simple analgesics early; triptans (5-HT1B/1D agonists) for moderate-severe attacks; antiemetics (dopamine antagonists).
Prevention if frequent: beta-blockers, certain anticonvulsants, tricyclic antidepressants, or CGRP-targeting monoclonal antibodies.
Lifestyle: regular sleep, meals, hydration; limit painkiller days to avoid medication-overuse headache.
cases.pearl: SNOOP red flags: Systemic signs, Neuro deficit, Onset sudden (thunderclap), Older age, Pattern change. None here, so no scan.

cases.cc: Fever, cough with rusty phlegm, and it hurts on the right side when I breathe.
cases.vit: T 39.1 °C · HR 112 · BP 108/66 · RR 26 · SpO₂ 89% on room air
hx: How long has he been sick?
3 days; started suddenly with shaking chills.
What does the phlegm look like?
His wife says he's slower today.
ex: Listen to the right lower chest
Dull over the right lower lobe.
Increased on the right (solid lung transmits vibration).
tx: Dense consolidation of the right lower lobe with air bronchograms.
No clot. Not needed: X-ray already explains it.
cases.patho: Streptococcus pneumoniae from the upper airway reaches the alveoli and multiplies. Its capsule resists phagocytosis. Alveoli fill with fluid, neutrophils, red cells and fibrin (red hepatisation, then grey hepatisation), so a whole lobe becomes solid: dull to percuss, transmits sound (bronchial breathing). Blood keeps flowing past airless alveoli (shunt), causing hypoxemia. Inflamed pleura gives pleuritic pain; red cells in sputum give the rust colour.
tr: Antibiotics: for a hospitalised patient, a beta-lactam plus a macrolide (or a respiratory fluoroquinolone class).
Oxygen, IV fluids, fever control; ICU if CURB-65 is high or oxygen can't be maintained.
Prevention: pneumococcal and flu vaccines, quit smoking.
cases.pearl: CURB-65: Confusion, Urea >7, Resp rate ≥30, BP low, age ≥65. He scores 3 = admit.

cases.cc: Crushing chest pain, like an elephant sitting on me, for 40 minutes.
hx: Down the left arm and into the jaw.
Smoker, high cholesterol, father had a heart attack at 52.
Does it change with breathing or position?
tx: ST elevation in leads II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL: inferior STEMI.
Not needed: ECG explains it, and it delays treatment.
cases.patho: A cholesterol-rich atherosclerotic plaque in the right coronary artery ruptures. Exposed collagen and tissue factor trigger platelets to stick and clump, and a clot completely blocks the artery. Downstream heart muscle (here the inferior wall, seen in leads II, III, aVF) loses oxygen; full-thickness (transmural) ischemia causes ST elevation. Without reperfusion, cells die from inside out over hours. Dying cells release troponin. Ischemic tissue can trigger dangerous arrhythmias (the main early cause of death).
tr: Reperfusion fast: percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI, a stent) within 90 minutes of first contact; thrombolytics if PCI isn't available in time.
Antiplatelets (aspirin plus a P2Y12 inhibitor), anticoagulation (heparins), nitrates for pain if BP allows (avoid in right ventricular infarct), beta-blockers, statins.
Later: ACE inhibitors, cardiac rehab, stop smoking.
cases.pearl: Inferior MI: check right-sided leads. Right ventricular infarct = nitrates can crash the BP.

cases.cc: I can't breathe. My inhaler isn't working.
hx: Yes, since age 6. One ICU stay two years ago.
A cold this week, and they were cleaning out a dusty garage.
Every hour since noon, barely helping.
Supposed to, but stopped a month ago.
Choking on food or a toy?
ex: Only 2–3 words at a time: severe.
Look at the neck and chest
Using neck muscles, sucking in between ribs (retractions).
tx: CO₂ normal (4.9 kPa). A NORMAL CO₂ in a kid breathing this fast means he's tiring: worrying.
Hyperinflated, no pneumothorax. (Reasonable if not improving.)
Useful later, never during an attack.
cases.patho: Triggers (viral infection, dust allergens) activate mast cells and Th2 inflammation in the airways. Histamine and leukotrienes contract airway smooth muscle; inflammation swells the walls and plugs them with mucus. Narrow airways slam shut on breathing out, trapping air (hyperinflation, wheeze, long expiration). Ventilation-perfusion mismatch causes hypoxemia. At first CO₂ is low from fast breathing; a 'normal' or rising CO₂ means exhaustion and impending respiratory failure.
tr: Short-acting beta-2 agonists (salbutamol/albuterol) back-to-back by nebuliser or spacer, plus an inhaled anticholinergic (ipratropium).
Systemic corticosteroids early (oral or IV) to calm the inflammation.
Oxygen to keep SpO₂ 94–98%; IV magnesium or IV bronchodilators if not improving; ICU if tiring.
Afterwards: restart the inhaled corticosteroid preventer and an asthma action plan.
cases.pearl: A silent chest (no wheeze because little air moves) is a life-threatening sign, not an improvement.

cases.cc: I'm exhausted all the time, always cold, and I've gained weight.
hx: How long has this been going on?
Dry skin, hair thinning, outer eyebrows thinning.
ex: Look at the face and skin
Puffy face, dry coarse skin, non-pitting swelling (myxedema).
tx: Not needed for a diffuse goitre without nodules.
Only if TSH were LOW with low T4 (pituitary cause).
cases.patho: In Hashimoto thyroiditis, T cells and antibodies (anti-TPO, anti-thyroglobulin) slowly destroy thyroid follicles. Less T4 and T3 are made. The pituitary senses low thyroid hormone and pumps out more TSH (negative feedback), which can enlarge the gland. Thyroid hormone sets the body's metabolic rate, so everything slows: heat production (cold), heart rate, gut motility (constipation), thinking, and reflex relaxation. Glycosaminoglycans accumulate in skin, causing myxedema.
tr: Thyroid hormone replacement: levothyroxine (synthetic T4), adjusted every 6–8 weeks by TSH.
Start low and go slow in older people or heart disease.
Recheck TSH yearly once stable.
cases.pearl: TSH is the best screening test. High TSH + low T4 = primary. Low/normal TSH + low T4 = central (pituitary).

cases.cc: My right hand shakes when I'm resting and I'm getting slower.
cases.vit: T 36.8 °C · HR 70 · BP 128/78 (drops to 104/70 standing) · RR 14 · SpO₂ 98%
hx: At rest, like rolling a pill between his fingers; it goes away when he reaches for something.
His wife says he punches in his sleep (REM sleep behaviour disorder).
ex: Small shuffling steps, reduced right arm swing, turns in many steps.
tx: Parkinson disease is diagnosed from the exam: bradykinesia plus rest tremor or rigidity.
Reduced uptake in the putamen, worse on the left. Only needed if the diagnosis is unclear.
Normal. Done if signs are atypical.
cases.patho: Dopamine-producing neurons of the substantia nigra pars compacta (in the midbrain) die, with clumps of misfolded alpha-synuclein called Lewy bodies. Symptoms appear after about 60–80% are lost. Less dopamine in the striatum unbalances the basal ganglia circuits: the indirect 'brake' pathway wins over the direct 'go' pathway, so movement becomes small and slow. Smell loss and REM sleep behaviour disorder can start years earlier because synuclein pathology begins in the olfactory bulb and lower brainstem.
tr: Dopamine replacement: levodopa combined with a dopa-decarboxylase inhibitor (carbidopa).
Dopamine agonists, MAO-B inhibitors and COMT inhibitors extend the effect.
Deep brain stimulation (electrodes in the subthalamic nucleus or GPi) for advanced fluctuations: a neurosurgery procedure.
Physio and exercise help gait and balance.
cases.pearl: Rest tremor that's asymmetric = Parkinson. Action tremor in both hands that improves with alcohol = essential tremor.
